result: Many viruses across all three domains of life (bacteriophages, archaeoviruses, and eukaryotic viruses) have pressurized genomes inside their capsids, with pressures reaching tens of atmospheres. This pressure results from tight confinement of negatively charged double-stranded viral DNA or dsRNA inside the capsid.
evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work (Evilevitch et al., 2003; Hanhijärvi et al., 2013; Bauer et al., 2013; Tzlil et al., 2003; Kindt et al., 2001; Purohit et al., 2005). These claims establish the background knowledge about pressurized viral genomes and are appropriately attributed to previous studies.

result: HSV-1 capsid contains DNA pressure of 20 atmospheres, representing the first demonstration of a pressurized genome state in a eukaryotic virus.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10 are supported by citation to prior measurement by Bauer et al., 2013. This establishes the foundation for the current work and is appropriately attributed to previous research by the same group.

result: High internal capsid pressure is generated by an ATP-driven packaging motor at a unique capsid vertex, which is the strongest molecular motor known. Structural features of packaging motor components are shared across bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic viruses, suggesting that pressure-driven genome release is a central mechanism of viral replication.
evaluation: Claims C11-C14 are supported by citations to McElwee et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2001; and Krupovic and Bamford, 2011. The inference about pressure-driven genome release being central to viral replication (C14) is reasonable given the shared structural features, though it remains a hypothesis to be tested.

result: Previous attempts to demonstrate pressure-driven DNA ejection in bacteriophages were inconclusive due to large cell-to-cell variability in ejection rates. The role of high DNA pressure in viral genome delivery remained unclear for both bacterial and eukaryotic viral infections.
evaluation: Claims C15-C23 accurately assess the state of knowledge in the field based on citations to Van Valen et al., 2012 and Evilevitch, 2018. These claims establish the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

result: The mechanism of osmotic suppression is explained: viral capsids are permeable to water and small ions, and water is drawn into the capsid due to high DNA concentration, developing large osmotic pressure. Addition of osmolyte creates an osmotic gradient that draws water out, reducing pressure inside the capsid. At critical osmolyte concentration c*, the pressure inside equals atmospheric pressure, eliminating the driving force for DNA ejection.
evaluation: Claims C45-C55 describe the thermodynamic mechanism of osmotic suppression, supported by citations to Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003; and Evilevitch et al., 2008. The explanation is based on established principles of osmotic pressure and is logically consistent.

result: PEG 8 kDa was used to create osmotic pressure gradient because it does not permeate the HSV-1 capsid (pore diameter ~20 Å, ~4 kDa MW cutoff). DNA ejection was triggered by mild trypsin treatment that cleaves portal proteins UL6 and UL25. At 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa, the external osmotic pressure of ~18 atm matches and 'turns off' the DNA pressure in the HSV-1 capsid.
evaluation: Claims C56-C63 describe the experimental design for osmotic suppression. The choice of PEG 8 kDa is well-justified based on capsid pore size (C57, supported by Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003). The trypsin treatment method is supported by citations to Bauer et al., 2013; Newcomb et al., 2007. The critical PEG concentration determination (C62) is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

result: Individual GFP-labeled HSV-1 C-capsids bind specifically to NPCs on isolated cell nuclei, as visualized by SR-SIM and confocal microscopy. Tegument-free C-capsids bind efficiently to NPCs and can eject DNA. WGA blocks NPC and prevents capsid binding, demonstrating binding specificity. Capsid-NPC binding is not inhibited by 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa.
evaluation: Claims C64-C72 are supported by SR-SIM and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3. The WGA control (C70-C71) appropriately demonstrates binding specificity. The finding that PEG does not inhibit capsid binding (C72) is important for interpreting subsequent ejection experiments. The consistency with prior work (C68, citing Ojala et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2014) strengthens the findings.

result: The reconstituted nuclei system maintains integrity and full NPC transport functionality at ~18 atm osmotic pressure generated by PEG. Under hyperosmotic conditions, nuclei slightly shrink but sub-nuclear DNA structure remains unchanged. NPC transport of GST-NLS-EGFP protein is maintained, demonstrating that the system provides a robust assay for investigating viral DNA ejection under hyperosmotic conditions.
evaluation: Claims C73-C82 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: citation to Finan et al., 2011 showing NPC functionality is maintained under hyperosmotic stress (C73-C76), DAPI staining showing nuclear structure is preserved (C77-C78, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), dextran exclusion assay showing nuclear integrity (C79, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and NLS transport assay demonstrating active transport through NPCs (C80-C81). These validation experiments are critical for interpreting the main results.

result: Using a pull-down assay with qPCR quantification, ~98% of HSV-1 capsids bound to nuclei ejected their DNA without osmolyte addition. When capsid pressure is turned off at 18 atm external osmotic pressure (30% w/w PEG 8 kDa), DNA ejection is completely suppressed (~0.2% ejection). Total DNA remains constant with and without PEG, confirming that the reduction in ejected DNA is due to suppression of ejection, not DNA loss during fractionation.
evaluation: Claims C83-C93 present the core experimental results using the pull-down assay. The qPCR data in Figure 5 clearly show nearly complete DNA ejection without PEG (C83) and complete suppression with PEG (C87). The control showing total DNA remains constant (C91-C93, Figure 5C) is essential for ruling out DNA loss as an alternative explanation. The pull-down assay efficiency is validated at 94-99% (C85). The primer design (C88-C90) allows detection of both complete and partial ejection. These results directly test the hypothesis that capsid pressure drives DNA ejection.

result: PEG addition does not interfere with capsid binding to nuclei; in fact, the number of capsids bound to nuclei is slightly increased with 30% PEG, possibly due to crowding effects. Free viral DNA from broken capsids (fraction a) is reduced by PEG but represents less than 0.2% of total DNA.
evaluation: Claims C94-C99 are supported by fluorescence microscopy (C94, Figure 3B) and qPCR data (C95, Figure 5B). The interpretation of enhanced binding due to crowding effects (C96) is reasonable and supported by citation to Minton, 2006. The observation about fraction a (C97-C99) is important for ruling out artifacts from broken capsids.

result: Electron microscopy visualization confirms the pull-down assay results. At 4°C without ATP, ~95% of capsids retain DNA (negative control). At 37°C without PEG, ~62% of capsids eject DNA. With 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa, ~81% of capsids retain DNA. Capsids bind in multilayer clusters, with only the first layer able to dock to NPCs and eject DNA. The pull-down assay shows even higher fractions because it specifically isolates NPC-bound capsids.
evaluation: Claims C100-C107 are supported by EM data in Figure 6. The negative control at 4°C (C100) appropriately demonstrates that the experimental conditions can prevent ejection. The quantification of DNA-filled vs. empty capsids (C101, C104) provides independent validation of the pull-down assay results. The observation about multilayer binding (C103) explains why not all capsids eject DNA in the positive control. The comparison between EM and pull-down assay (C105-C107) is reasonable and strengthens confidence in both methods.

result: Control experiments with PEG 400 Da demonstrate that DNA ejection suppression is caused by osmotic pressure gradient across the capsid wall, not by PEG blocking the NPC channel. PEG 400 Da generates 18 atm osmotic pressure but permeates the capsid, so no pressure gradient is created. With PEG 400 Da, ~60% of capsids eject DNA, equivalent to the no-PEG control, confirming that the osmotic pressure gradient mechanism is responsible for suppression.
evaluation: Claims C108-C115 describe a critical control experiment that rules out alternative explanations. The logic is sound: PEG 400 Da generates the same osmotic pressure as PEG 8 kDa but permeates the capsid (C111, based on capsid pore size), so it cannot create a pressure gradient (C112). The EM data showing equivalent ejection with PEG 400 Da and without PEG (C113-C114, Figure 6) strongly supports the conclusion that the osmotic pressure gradient mechanism is responsible for suppression (C115). This control is essential for the main conclusion.

result: The combined pull-down assay and EM data demonstrate that viral DNA ejection from HSV-1 capsids into host nuclei is completely blocked when intracapsid genome pressure is turned off through osmolyte addition. This proves that viral DNA translocation from herpesvirus capsids across the nuclear membrane is driven by intracapsid pressure, and that capsid pressure is critical for initiation of DNA ejection into a host nucleus.
evaluation: Claims C116-C117, C3, C24, and C123 state the main conclusion of the study. This conclusion is well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches: osmotic suppression assay (Figure 2), pull-down assay with qPCR (Figure 5), EM visualization (Figure 6), and critical controls with PEG 400 Da. The logic is sound: if capsid pressure drives ejection, then eliminating the pressure should prevent ejection, which is exactly what is observed. The ~98% ejection without PEG vs. ~0.2% with PEG provides strong quantitative support.

result: This work provides the first demonstration of a pressure-dependent mechanism of viral genome penetration into a host nucleus leading to infection of eukaryotic cells. Despite previous measurements of intracapsid DNA pressure, the role of capsid pressure for intranuclear viral genome delivery had not been demonstrated until now.
evaluation: Claims C4, C121, and C122 assert the novelty of the findings. The claim of being 'first' is supported by the assessment of prior work (C15-C23) showing that previous attempts were inconclusive. The experimental demonstration is rigorous and addresses the key question directly. However, the claim should be qualified as demonstrating the role of pressure in 'initiation' of ejection, as the authors acknowledge that other factors may contribute to complete genome internalization (C124).

result: While capsid pressure is critical for initiation of DNA ejection, other factors may contribute to complete internalization of the viral genome. Capsid pressure rapidly decreases with increasing ejected DNA fraction, and at cellular osmotic pressures (3-4 atm), only ~50% of DNA is ejected. DNA condensation in the crowded cellular environment exerts a pulling force that facilitates complete internalization, potentially through a two-step process.
evaluation: Claims C124-C131 appropriately acknowledge limitations and propose mechanisms for complete genome internalization. The observation that pressure decreases with ejection (C125, Figure 2) and that only ~50% ejects at cellular osmotic pressure (C126) is data-supported. The discussion of DNA condensation and pulling forces (C129-C130) is supported by citations to prior work (Parsegian et al., 2000; Jeembaeva et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2018). This nuanced discussion strengthens the paper by acknowledging that pressure-driven ejection may be necessary but not sufficient for complete genome delivery.

result: High intracapsid DNA packing density resulting in tens of atmospheres of pressure is a distinctive trait of all nine human herpesviruses. Calculated capsid DNA pressures range from ~14 atm for VZV to ~90 atm for EBV, related to variation in DNA packing density. This strongly suggests that pressure-driven entry of viral DNA into the host nucleus is universal to all herpesviruses.
evaluation: Claims C132-C137 extend the findings to other herpesviruses through calculations. The calculations (C133, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) are based on established theoretical models (Tzlil et al., 2003; Purohit et al., 2003) and EM-measured capsid dimensions (Booy et al., 1991; Germi et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2017). The calculated HSV-1 pressure agrees with measured values (C134), validating the approach. The inference that pressure-driven entry is universal to herpesviruses (C137) is reasonable given that all have high DNA packing density, though direct experimental validation for other herpesviruses would strengthen this claim.

result: The findings may extend to other viruses beyond herpesviruses. Reoviruses replicate ssRNA to dsRNA inside the capsid, resulting in high packing density that could regulate intracapsid replication. HIV capsids dock to NPCs and release dsDNA, with reverse transcription associated with increasing internal pressure. This work provides a platform for analysis of pressure-regulated replication in many viruses.
evaluation: Claims C138-C142 appropriately extend the implications to other viral systems. The examples of reoviruses (C138, citing Prasad et al., 1996) and HIV (C140-C141, citing Rankovic et al., 2017) are supported by citations. The speculation about pressure-regulated replication in reoviruses (C139) is clearly presented as a hypothesis. The claim that this work provides a platform for broader analysis (C142) is reasonable given the methods developed.

result: Herpesviridae are a leading cause of human viral disease, second only to influenza and cold viruses. Nine herpesviruses are human pathogens causing life-long infections with latency periods. Infections can cause oral and genital lesions, encephalitis, shingles, birth defects, transplant failures, and oncogenic transformation.
evaluation: Claims C25-C32 provide background on the medical importance of herpesviruses. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to authoritative sources (Pellett and Roizmann, 2007; Roizmann et al., 2007; Sandri-Goldin, 2006; Davison et al., 2009; Pai and Weinberger, 2017; Coen, 2006; Rickinson and Kieff, 2007; Ganem, 2007). This background establishes the significance of understanding herpesvirus infection mechanisms.

result: Herpesviruses consist of dsDNA genome packaged in an icosahedral capsid surrounded by tegument and lipid envelope. After cell entry, capsids are transported to the nucleus and eject their genome upon docking to NPCs. HSV-1 is a prototypical model system for studying herpesvirus replication due to ease of growing and purifying C-capsids.
evaluation: Claims C33-C36, C43-C44 provide essential background on herpesvirus structure and infection process. The structural description (C33) is based on established knowledge. The infection process (C34-C35) is supported by EM images in Figure 1 and citation to Sodeik et al., 1997. The choice of HSV-1 as a model system (C44) is well-justified and supported by citation to Méndez-Álvarez, 2000.

result: DNA ejection from isolated HSV-1 capsids can be suppressed by creating osmotic pressure that matches the packaged DNA pressure, effectively eliminating genome pressure. The reconstituted nuclei system accurately reproduces capsid-nuclei binding and nuclear transport, providing the benefit of isolating the effect of eliminated capsid pressure on DNA ejection while avoiding interference from hyperosmotic conditions on other cellular processes.
evaluation: Claims C38-C42 describe the experimental strategy. The osmotic suppression approach (C38-C39) is supported by citation to prior work (Bauer et al., 2013). The validity of the reconstituted nuclei system (C41) is supported by multiple citations (Ojala et al., 2000; Adam et al., 1990; Au et al., 2016; Cassany and Gerace, 2008). The rationale for using this system (C42) is sound and addresses potential concerns about artifacts from hyperosmotic conditions.

result: Cytosol contains importin-β required for capsid binding to NPCs. The ATP-regeneration system is required for opening the capsid portal but not for binding. Import protein factors (importin-β, Ran-GTP cycle) are involved in capsid binding and portal opening but do not provide the driving force for DNA translocation across the NPC channel, which is driven by capsid pressure.
evaluation: Claims C143-C150 describe the molecular requirements for the reconstituted system. The roles of cytosol, importin-β, and ATP are supported by citations to Ojala et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2014; Cole and Hammell, 1998; Cautain et al., 2015; Macara, 2001; Flatt and Greber, 2015. The inference that import factors trigger ejection but don't drive translocation (C149-C150) is reasonable and consistent with the experimental findings showing that pressure is required for ejection.

result: All eukaryotic DNA viruses except poxviruses deliver and replicate their genomes within the nucleus. Retroviruses also transport genomes across nuclear membranes after reverse transcription. The mechanism of viral DNA entry into the host nucleus remains poorly understood for most viruses.
evaluation: Claims C118-C120 provide broader context for the significance of the work. All claims are supported by citation to Hennig and O'Hare, 2015, and C119 is based on established knowledge of retrovirus replication. This context appropriately frames the importance of understanding nuclear entry mechanisms.
